title: Universal Properties
---

Many constructions in mathematics are characterized not by explicit formulas but by *universal properties*—conditions that specify the construction uniquely up to isomorphism. We’ve already seen this with quotient spaces: the quotient $V/U$ is characterized by the fact that any linear map that kills $U$ factors uniquely through it. Products and coproducts provide two more fundamental examples.

## <span class="num">8.3.1</span> Products and Coproducts

:::definition{8.3.1} Product
Let $\mcC$ be a category and $A, B \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mcC)$. A ***product*** of $A$ and $B$ is an object $P$ together with morphisms $\pi_1 : P \to A$ and $\pi_2 : P \to B$ (called ***projections***) satisfying the following ***universal property***:

For any object $T$ and morphisms $\alpha : T \to A$, $\beta : T \to B$, there exists a *unique* morphism $\varphi : T \to P$ such that $\pi_1 \circ \varphi = \alpha$ and $\pi_2 \circ \varphi = \beta$.

![fig-8-3-1](/notes/math-55a/figures/fig-8-3-1.svg)

We write $P = A \times B$ and $\varphi = (\alpha, \beta)$ for the unique induced map.
:::

:::note
The universal property says: to give a map into the product is the same as giving a map into each factor. This is the categorical abstraction of the familiar fact that a function $f : T \to A \times B$ is determined by its components $f_1 = \pi_1 \circ f$ and $f_2 = \pi_2 \circ f$.
:::

The dual notion reverses all arrows.

:::definition{8.3.2} Coproduct
Let $\mcC$ be a category and $A, B \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mcC)$. A ***coproduct*** (or ***sum***) of $A$ and $B$ is an object $S$ together with morphisms $\iota_1 : A \to S$ and $\iota_2 : B \to S$ (called ***inclusions*** or ***coprojections***) satisfying:

For any object $T$ and morphisms $\alpha : A \to T$, $\beta : B \to T$, there exists a *unique* morphism $\varphi : S \to T$ such that $\varphi \circ \iota_1 = \alpha$ and $\varphi \circ \iota_2 = \beta$.

![fig-8-3-2](/notes/math-55a/figures/fig-8-3-2.svg)

We write $S = A \amalg B$ or $A + B$ and $\varphi = [\alpha, \beta]$ for the unique induced map.
:::

:::note
The universal property of the coproduct says: to give a map out of the coproduct is the same as giving a map out of each summand. This duality between products and coproducts—reversing all arrows—is a general phenomenon in category theory.
:::

:::theorem{8.3.3} Uniqueness of products and coproducts
If a product (resp. coproduct) of $A$ and $B$ exists, it is unique up to unique isomorphism. That is, if $(P, \pi_1, \pi_2)$ and $(P', \pi_1', \pi_2')$ are both products of $A$ and $B$, then there is a unique isomorphism $\psi : P \to P'$ with $\pi_1' \circ \psi = \pi_1$ and $\pi_2' \circ \psi = \pi_2$; and similarly for coproducts.
:::

:::proof
By the universal property of $P'$, applied to the maps $\pi_1 : P \to A$ and $\pi_2 : P \to B$, there exists a unique $\psi : P \to P'$ with $\pi_1' \circ \psi = \pi_1$ and $\pi_2' \circ \psi = \pi_2$.

By the universal property of $P$, applied to $\pi_1' : P' \to A$ and $\pi_2' : P' \to B$, there exists a unique $\psi' : P' \to P$ with $\pi_1 \circ \psi' = \pi_1'$ and $\pi_2 \circ \psi' = \pi_2'$.

Now $\psi' \circ \psi : P \to P$ satisfies $\pi_1 \circ (\psi' \circ \psi) = \pi_1$ and $\pi_2 \circ (\psi' \circ \psi) = \pi_2$. But $\id_P$ also satisfies these equations. By uniqueness in the universal property of $P$ (applied to $T = P$, $\alpha = \pi_1$, $\beta = \pi_2$), we have $\psi' \circ \psi = \id_P$. Similarly, $\psi \circ \psi' = \id_{P'}$. So $\psi$ is an isomorphism, and it is the only morphism with $\pi_1' \circ \psi = \pi_1$ and $\pi_2' \circ \psi = \pi_2$.

The proof for coproducts is the same with all arrows reversed.
:::

:::note
This proof pattern—using universal properties to construct inverse maps—is standard in category theory. The key is that universal properties give *uniqueness*, which forces the composites to be identities.
:::

Products and coproducts need not exist in every category. When working in a new category, one of the first questions is whether these constructions exist and what form they take.

## <span class="num">8.3.2</span> Products and Coproducts in Familiar Categories

:::example{8.3.4} Products and coproducts in $\mathbf{Set}$
In the category of sets:

- The **product** $A \times B$ is the Cartesian product $\{(a, b) : a \in A, b \in B\}$ with projections $\pi_1(a, b) = a$ and $\pi_2(a, b) = b$.
- The **coproduct** $A \amalg B$ is the disjoint union $A \sqcup B = \{(a, 1) : a \in A\} \cup \{(b, 2) : b \in B\}$ with inclusions $\iota_1(a) = (a, 1)$ and $\iota_2(b) = (b, 2)$.

For the coproduct, given $\alpha : A \to T$ and $\beta : B \to T$, the only possible $\varphi$ is $\varphi(a, 1) = \alpha(a)$, $\varphi(b, 2) = \beta(b)$. The product case is Exercise [8.3](/notes/math-55a/8-3-universal-properties)(1).
:::

:::example{8.3.5} Products and coproducts in $\mathbf{Grp}$
In the category of groups:

- The **product** $G \times H$ is the direct product, with componentwise operations and the two projections.
- The **coproduct** $G * H$ is the ***free product***, a more complicated construction whose elements are reduced words alternating between nonidentity elements of $G$ and of $H$. Exercise [8.3](/notes/math-55a/8-3-universal-properties)(2) treats the case $G = H = \ZZ$, where it is the free group on two generators (Section [3.6](/notes/math-55a/3-6-free-groups-and-presentations)).

In the subcategory $\mathbf{Ab}$ of abelian groups, both the product and the coproduct of $G$ and $H$ are the direct sum $G \oplus H = G \times H$ (the same group, with different universal properties: projections for the product, inclusions for the coproduct).
:::

:::example{8.3.6} Products and coproducts in $\mathbf{Vect}_k$
In $\mathbf{Vect}_k$ (and also in $\mathbf{FinVect}_k$), both the product and the coproduct of $V$ and $W$ are realized by the **direct sum** $V \oplus W$.

**As a product:** Define $\pi_1 : V \oplus W \to V$ by $\pi_1(v, w) = v$ and $\pi_2 : V \oplus W \to W$ by $\pi_2(v, w) = w$. Given linear maps $\alpha : T \to V$ and $\beta : T \to W$, define $\varphi : T \to V \oplus W$ by $\varphi(t) = (\alpha(t), \beta(t))$. It is linear, and it is the unique map with $\pi_1 \circ \varphi = \alpha$ and $\pi_2 \circ \varphi = \beta$, since these two conditions specify both components of $\varphi(t)$.

**As a coproduct:** Define $\iota_1 : V \to V \oplus W$ by $\iota_1(v) = (v, 0)$ and $\iota_2 : W \to V \oplus W$ by $\iota_2(w) = (0, w)$. Given linear maps $\alpha : V \to T$ and $\beta : W \to T$, define $\varphi : V \oplus W \to T$ by $\varphi(v, w) = \alpha(v) + \beta(w)$. It is linear and satisfies $\varphi \circ \iota_1 = \alpha$ and $\varphi \circ \iota_2 = \beta$. It is the only such map: any linear $\varphi'$ with these properties satisfies $$\varphi'(v, w) = \varphi'(\iota_1(v) + \iota_2(w)) = \alpha(v) + \beta(w).$$
:::

:::note
The coincidence of products and coproducts in $\mathbf{Vect}_k$ (and $\mathbf{Ab}$) reflects the additive structure of these categories: morphisms can be added, which is what the formula $\alpha(v) + \beta(w)$ uses. In categories without such structure (like $\mathbf{Set}$ or $\mathbf{Grp}$), products and coproducts are genuinely different constructions.
:::

:::exercise{8.3.7} Products and coproducts
<!-- list:paren-decimal -->

1. Verify explicitly that the Cartesian product satisfies the universal property of products in $\mathbf{Set}$.
2. Show that in $\mathbf{Ab}$, the coproduct of $\ZZ$ and $\ZZ$ is $\ZZ^2$, while in $\mathbf{Grp}$, it is the free group $F_2$ on two generators.
3. Let $V$ and $W$ be finite-dimensional vector spaces over $k$. Show that $\dim(V \oplus W) = \dim V + \dim W$ using only the universal property of $V \oplus W$ as a coproduct (not by direct computation).

:::solution
**(1)** Let $A, B$ be sets and let $T$ be any set with functions $\alpha : T \to A$ and $\beta : T \to B$. We must show there exists a unique function $\varphi : T \to A \times B$ with $\pi_1 \circ \varphi = \alpha$ and $\pi_2 \circ \varphi = \beta$.

*Existence:* Define $\varphi(t) = (\alpha(t), \beta(t))$. Then $\pi_1(\varphi(t)) = \alpha(t)$ and $\pi_2(\varphi(t)) = \beta(t)$.

*Uniqueness:* If $\psi : T \to A \times B$ satisfies $\pi_1 \circ \psi = \alpha$ and $\pi_2 \circ \psi = \beta$, then for any $t \in T$, $\psi(t) = (\pi_1(\psi(t)), \pi_2(\psi(t))) = (\alpha(t), \beta(t)) = \varphi(t)$.

**(2)** In $\mathbf{Ab}$: take $S = \ZZ^2$ with $\iota_1(n) = (n, 0)$ and $\iota_2(n) = (0, n)$. Let $A$ be an abelian group and $\alpha, \beta : \ZZ \to A$ homomorphisms. Define $\varphi : \ZZ^2 \to A$ by $\varphi(m, n) = m\,\alpha(1) + n\,\beta(1)$. This is a homomorphism because $A$ is abelian (the terms can be rearranged), and $\varphi(\iota_1(m)) = m\,\alpha(1) = \alpha(m)$, $\varphi(\iota_2(n)) = \beta(n)$. It is unique: any homomorphism $\varphi'$ with $\varphi' \circ \iota_1 = \alpha$ and $\varphi' \circ \iota_2 = \beta$ satisfies $\varphi'(m, n) = \varphi'(m, 0) + \varphi'(0, n) = \alpha(m) + \beta(n) = \varphi(m, n)$.

In $\mathbf{Grp}$: the coproduct must accommodate non-commuting images. A homomorphism $\alpha : \ZZ \to G$ is determined by $g = \alpha(1)$, since $\alpha(n) = g^n$, and every $g \in G$ arises this way. Let $F_2$ be the free group on $\{a, b\}$, with $\iota_1(n) = a^n$ and $\iota_2(n) = b^n$. Given $\alpha, \beta : \ZZ \to G$, put $g = \alpha(1)$ and $h = \beta(1)$. By the universal property of free groups (Section [3.6](/notes/math-55a/3-6-free-groups-and-presentations)), there is a unique homomorphism $\varphi : F_2 \to G$ with $\varphi(a) = g$ and $\varphi(b) = h$. Then $\varphi(\iota_1(n)) = g^n = \alpha(n)$ and $\varphi(\iota_2(n)) = h^n = \beta(n)$. Conversely, any $\varphi'$ with $\varphi' \circ \iota_1 = \alpha$ and $\varphi' \circ \iota_2 = \beta$ has $\varphi'(a) = g$ and $\varphi'(b) = h$, so $\varphi' = \varphi$. Hence $(F_2, \iota_1, \iota_2)$ is a coproduct of $\ZZ$ and $\ZZ$ in $\mathbf{Grp}$. (The group $\ZZ^2$ is not, since $g$ and $h$ need not commute.)

**(3)** We use the following characterization of bases, which involves only maps out of $U$.

*Claim.* Let $U$ be a vector space and $(u_s)_{s \in S}$ a family of vectors in $U$. Then $(u_s)$ is a basis of $U$ consisting of distinct vectors iff for every vector space $T$ and every function $f : S \to T$ there is a unique linear map $L : U \to T$ with $L(u_s) = f(s)$ for all $s \in S$.

*Proof of the claim.* If $(u_s)$ is a basis of distinct vectors, this is the familiar fact that a linear map can be prescribed arbitrarily on a basis, and is determined by these values. Conversely, assume the property. *Spanning:* let $U' = \operatorname{span}(u_s)$, and compare the quotient map $q : U \to U/U'$ (Definition [7.1.1](/notes/math-55a/7-1-quotient-spaces#definition-7-1-1)) with the zero map $U \to U/U'$; both send every $u_s$ to $0$, so by uniqueness $q = 0$, i.e., $U' = U$. *Independence and distinctness:* let $T$ be a vector space with a basis $(\delta_s)_{s \in S}$ (for instance the space of finitely supported functions $S \to k$), and let $L$ be the linear map with $L(u_s) = \delta_s$. If $\sum_s c_s u_s = 0$ (a finite sum), applying $L$ gives $\sum_s c_s \delta_s = 0$, so all $c_s = 0$; and $u_s = u_{s'}$ forces $\delta_s = \delta_{s'}$, so $s = s'$. This proves the claim.

Now let $(v_i)_{i \in I}$ be a basis of $V$ and $(w_j)_{j \in J}$ a basis of $W$, with $|I| = \dim V$ and $|J| = \dim W$. Consider the family of $|I| + |J|$ vectors of $V \oplus W$ indexed by the disjoint union $I \sqcup J$: $\iota_1(v_i)$ for $i \in I$ and $\iota_2(w_j)$ for $j \in J$. Let $T$ be any vector space and $f : I \sqcup J \to T$ any function. By the claim for $V$ and $W$, there are unique linear maps $\alpha : V \to T$ and $\beta : W \to T$ with $\alpha(v_i) = f(i)$ and $\beta(w_j) = f(j)$. By the universal property of the coproduct, there is a unique linear $L : V \oplus W \to T$ with $L \circ \iota_1 = \alpha$ and $L \circ \iota_2 = \beta$. Thus $L(\iota_1(v_i)) = f(i)$ and $L(\iota_2(w_j)) = f(j)$. Any other linear $L'$ with these values satisfies $L' \circ \iota_1 = \alpha$ and $L' \circ \iota_2 = \beta$ (by uniqueness of $\alpha$ and $\beta$), hence $L' = L$. So the family has the property in the claim, and it is a basis of $V \oplus W$ consisting of $|I| + |J|$ distinct vectors. Therefore $\dim(V \oplus W) = \dim V + \dim W$.
:::
:::

:::note
The argument in (3) illustrates a general principle: universal properties translate into bijections of Hom-sets. For instance, the universal property of the coproduct says that $$\Hom(V \oplus W, T) \to \Hom(V, T) \times \Hom(W, T), \qquad L \mapsto (L \circ \iota_1, L \circ \iota_2),$$ is a bijection (it is even linear): the contravariant functor $\Hom(\cdot, T)$ of Example [8.2.6](/notes/math-55a/8-2-functors-and-natural-transformations#example-8-2-6) turns the coproduct $V \oplus W$ into a product.
:::
